newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan lawmaker, unions slam law revisions on women.
newsitem.headline: Japan lawmaker, unions slam law revisions on women.

text.p: Japanese labour unions and women's rights advocates on Thursday criticised changes to two laws on female employment as unsatisfactory and dangerous to working women.

Social Democrat legislator Sumiko Shimizu said a revision on Wednesday of Japan's 1986 Equal Employment Opportunity Law, intended to curb discrimination against women in hiring and promotion, was inadequate.
"The only thing which has changed is that the Labour Ministry can now publicly name a company which ignores its directives," she said.
"Apart from that there are no other penalties and the law does not force employers to tackle the problem," she added.
Shimizu, a member of Japan's Upper House of parliament, also criticised a revision of the 1947 Labour Standard Law that was strongly backed by business circles.

The change, which along with the equal opportunity amendment will go into effect in April 1999, will scrap limits on women working overtime and late at night, except for pregnant women and those with children.
The current law prohibits employers from requiring women to work between 10 p.m. and 5 a.m., except for certain workers such as airline cabin crews, nurses and broadcasters.
"Women will now have to deal with the responsibility of taking care of the children and the home and working badly paid late-night shifts. Many will be forced to quit," Shimizu said.

Japanese society, which prides itself on its work ethic, continues to struggle with the problem of "karoshi", or death through overwork, and the ubiquitous practice of unpaid overtime, National Confederation of Trade Unions spokesman Seiji Terama said.
Scrapping the limit on overtime to put women in the same position as men poses a threat to women's health, he added.
"Before we've only seen karoshi among men but it's likely that the phenomenon will spread to women after the new legislation is enacted," he said.
Notoriously long overtime hours, coupled with a lack of legal restraints on employers, creates a double danger, the union spokesman added.
"According to Labour Ministry figures the average worker puts in 147 hours of overtime per year, but our figures show that the actual number is more than three times that," he said.
"So scrapping the limit on overtime for women without putting a general ceiling on work hours exposes both male and female employees to overwork and abuse by employers," he added.
